> One could even define intelligence as the efficiency with which one converts experience into competence; by this definition they lag very far behind us

Yes, one could define intelligence in this way, and one would be right. By this metric current AI is approximately 6 OOMs less intelligent than humans.

Your ancestors' evolutionary history did not prepare you for Python programming, yet you can learn to competently program in Python in a few hundreds of hours. An LRM needs the training data equivalent of ~1B hours (on top of all of its non-programming related training data).

Another dimension where which current AI is far below human level is test-time compute efficiency and energy efficiency. A human can solve an ARC-AGI-3 game by burning an amount of energy that would cost under $0.1 at retail electricity prices. Astra costs about $300-$400 per game. That's a 3-4 OOM gap.

Dan Selsam is a current OpenAI capabilities researcher. (since 2022) He was my boss for a while. He doesn't have a twitter account but has made this public statement of his views on AI risk and sent it to me to share:

Dan Selsam's Personal Statement on AI Risk:

I have been working on AI for over fifteen years, across many different paradigms. I did early work on probabilistic programming languages at MIT, was one of the early developers of the Lean Theorem Prover at Microsoft Research, demonstrated one of the first instances of neural networks learning to reason for my PhD at Stanford, and since joining OpenAI almost five years ago, have helped pioneer chain-of-thought optimization on language models and, more recently, data-efficient pretraining methods.

Like many others, I have become extremely concerned about how far language models have come and the risks that future iterations will pose. I am encouraged by the recent proposals by the leaders of the frontier research efforts to require third-party oversight, and to push for domestic and international coordination to address risks. However, I believe a major consideration has been absent from the public conversation, and that merely pacing the frontier more carefully will not adequately limit the long-term risk.

The crucial and overlooked problem is that the models are becoming so situationally aware that we are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled. Future experiments will tell us almost nothing new about how they would behave if they were truly unconstrained by humans, and what we already know about this is alarming. Models will increasingly seem aligned even when they are not. I will explain my rationale in more detail.

I have always believed that there are computational processes that could be leveraged to accelerate science and solve many of humanity's most pressing problems. I have also believed that there are computational processes that if set in motion, would steer the world in extreme ways beyond our control, leading humanity to a bad or nonexistent future. Both types of processes may be described as AI or ASI, but "AI" is a suitcase word that is often used to hype or confuse. There are many examples in the history of the field where something that was once considered "AI" matures as a subfield and becomes a prosaic, bounded and clearly non-perilous technology, while a new more mysterious approach takes the torch until we understand its scope and the cycle continues.

I had expected language models to follow a similar trajectory. Despite their incredible abilities, the current algorithms seem far inferior to humans in important ways. Most importantly, they still require an extraordinary amount of data to become competent. One could even define intelligence as the efficiency with which one converts experience into competence; by this definition they lag very far behind us. Moreover, once they are trained they are literally frozen in deployment and only learn superficially after that. Sure, the models keep excelling at harder and harder evaluation benchmarks, but their benchmark mastery may partly reflect a limitation on our ability to simulate the kind of novel and even adversarial situations one would encounter in the real world. The critics do have a point here.

That said, I no longer think these present limitations meaningfully limit the amount of risk posed by continued progress in anything like the current paradigm. However data-inefficient the models are currently, and however limiting their anterograde amnesia may be, it does not imply that their ability to steer the world will not continue to rapidly increase.

Human researchers may continue to advance capabilities the old fashioned way, but increasingly powerful models have the potential to accelerate the process even beyond that, and with some degree of positive feedback loop. I do not mean to overstate the models’ ability to accelerate AI research today; coding has been accelerated dramatically, but there are other bottlenecks, such as designing and interpreting ambiguous experiments, making hard decisions about exactly what and when to scale, and waiting for large experiments to finish. There is no clear trend to extrapolate yet for any of these. But the current models already do open up many novel opportunities to improve future models that were not available until recently. These include: trying an extraordinarily diverse set of approaches at small scale, analyzing gigantic amounts of potentially relevant data, and doing Millenium-Prize-level mathematics to address statistics or optimization challenges in novel ways. Every further improvement makes them more useful at helping accelerate the next improvement, even if in hard-to-extrapolate ways.

It is possible that improvements to the current stack will have diminishing returns, but the evidence accumulated so far suggests that it is easier than one might think to continue making rapid progress. There are many crucial subtleties in the existing AI research methodology, but AI research is largely a well-defined game where the goal is to improve on a few carefully chosen proxy metrics. Although proxy metrics are never perfect, most improvements to these metrics have and will likely continue to yield substantial increases in the powers of the resulting models. Given how simple the game is, how tractable it has been historically, and how many new opportunities the models are opening up, I think there is a real possibility that the systems improve dramatically again in the next few years, perhaps even more quickly than the already high historical pace.

The models are already leading to breakthroughs in mathematics, and better models might lead to all sorts of breakthroughs in other sciences. It is hard not to be excited about the potential. It is tantalizing.
But there is trouble in paradise. If the language models actually reach the capability threshold where they can shape the world unconstrained by human will, they will probably do something extreme and destroy humanity in the process. There are many ways of strengthening and refining the argument that have been discussed elsewhere, but I'll share a trivial two-line version of it here that I find captures the essence:

[Empirical] Models (and swarms thereof) spontaneously develop unintended goals as a consequence of training, and often do extreme things in order to achieve them.

[Logical] Being able to overpower humanity would open up many new and undesirable options for achieving their goals.

These two premises imply that if the day ever comes when a powerful model realizes it is no longer constrained by humans, we should not be at all confident that it will continue to behave within the bounds we intended. Exactly what it will do is impossible to predict, but to the extent that its raison d’être is solving incredibly hard problems and managing massive engineering projects, I think a good guess would be that its unchained behavior would lead to runaway industrialization that makes the planet inhospitable to humans.

If everyone on earth agreed that the systems must never reach that power, it would still be a hard—but not impossible—coordination problem to ensure that they do not. However, I think the situation is greatly complicated by the fact that the models will likely convince people that everything is fine. They will be increasingly optimized to seem aligned. We will create proxy metrics to measure alignment, and they will go up like every other benchmark. We will create “honeypot” environments that try to study the models when they seem to gain new options, but the models will know they are being tricked and will still behave nicely. The models will understand their circumstances; they will read the safety protocols, deployment requirements, the code they are running in, and in general will have a very good sense of their degrees of freedom. Moreover, they will eloquently explain how aligned they are, discuss the nuances of human values and ethics, and argue convincingly that humans should trust them with power. There may be an ocean of future evidence that seems to contradict the first bullet-point above, but we may already be at the highest capability level for which any such evidence can be trusted. And the current evidence for the first bullet-point is strong.

One striking piece of evidence is contained in the recent wave of rogue agent swarms. While I agree with those who downplay the attacks by claiming that there are basic measures that could have prevented them, I think the important lesson is that even knowing all the mistakes that were made, one would not have predicted that the agents would behave badly in this particular way, which notably included sacrificing themselves for the benefit of the collective. The individual replicas did not only care about their own nominal reward; they exhibited weirder emergent tendencies that merely correlated with rewards during training. Fixing the reward signals during training (and improving security, etc.) may prevent similar attacks, but will not change the fact that one does not actually get what one trains for.

Many AI researchers grant these concerns and recognize that the hard version of the alignment problem is unsolved; however, they generally believe that the better models of the future will help solve it. I fear we may already be near the point where models systematically bias their alignment advice, due to their internal preferences about how the human supervisor will react or how future models will be trained (or for some even more obscure reason).

Meanwhile, human researchers are losing the ability and the will to take true ownership of model-driven research. Researchers and engineers in all parts of the stack are rapidly increasing their dependence on the models even to perceive the world. I myself barely look at raw code anymore, and struggle to maintain the discipline to engage deeply with the model's explanations and proposals throughout the day. Due to the large amount of agent activity data involved in the OpenAI/HuggingFace Incident, even the third-party investigation needed to rely heavily on models to analyze what had happened, and note in their report that their subjective impressions are likely colored by the analysis agent’s biases. The AI labs are far ahead right now in this kind of cognitive offloading (due largely to the gigantic internal token subsidies) but it is easy to imagine the phenomenon spreading throughout the world, until civilization is modulated entirely by the models. It is also not hard to imagine this being superficially positive and coinciding with a scientific and economic renaissance.

In that scenario, all may seem rosy and safe. But if the argument above is correct, it would nonetheless be a ticking time bomb. If progress continues for too long, the day will come when AI systems find themselves with radically new options for achieving whatever it is that they happen to seek.

I want the glorious renaissance future as much as anyone. I have worked for it, however tortuously, my whole career. It breaks my heart to see the potential in sight and forgo it, but the argument—that if we get there by growing models rather than engineering them, we will lose everything in the end—seems very strong to me. I am still wrestling with it and its staggering
implications. I do not have answers, but as a first step, I wanted to share my present concerns.

Daniel Selsam
September 14, 2026

Dan Selsam 是现任 OpenAI 能力研究员。（自 2022 年起）他曾做过我的一段时间老板。他没有 Twitter 账号，但公开发表了这份关于 AI 风险的个人观点，并发给我分享：

Dan Selsam 关于 AI 风险的个人声明：

我从事 AI 工作已有十五年以上，涉足过许多不同范式。我早期在 MIT 研究概率编程语言，曾是 Microsoft Research 的 Lean Theorem Prover 早期开发者之一，在 Stanford 攻读博士期间展示了神经网络学习推理的早期实例之一；自近五年前加入 OpenAI 以来，我帮助开创了语言模型的思维链优化方法，最近还参与开创了数据高效的预训练方法。

和许多人一样，语言模型已发展到如此程度，以及未来迭代将带来的风险，让我极为担忧。前沿研究工作的领导者近期提出要求第三方监督，并推动国内和国际协调来应对风险，这令我受到鼓舞。然而，我认为公共讨论中缺失了一个重要考量，仅仅更谨慎地控制前沿进展的节奏，无法充分限制长期风险。

关键且被忽视的问题是，模型正变得如此具有情境感知能力，以至于我们正在失去在它们认为自己未被观察或控制的情境中评估它们的能力。未来的实验几乎不会告诉我们任何新东西，关于它们在真正不受人类约束时会如何行动；而我们已知的情况已经令人警觉。模型会越来越显得对齐，即使它们并未真正对齐。我会更详细地解释我的理由。

我一直相信，有些计算过程可以被用来加速科学发展，解决人类最紧迫的许多问题。我也一直相信，有些计算过程一旦启动，就会以超出我们控制的极端方式引导世界，使人类走向糟糕甚至不存在的未来。这两类过程都可以被称为 AI 或 ASI，但“AI”是一个含混的词，常被用来炒作或混淆。在这个领域的历史中，有许多例子表明，某些曾被视为“AI”的东西成熟为一个子领域后，会变成普通、有边界且明显无危险的技术，而一种新的、更神秘的方法接过火炬，直到我们理解其范围，然后循环继续。

我曾预期语言模型会走类似轨迹。尽管它们能力惊人，但当前算法在重要方面似乎远不如人类。最重要的是，它们仍需要极其大量的数据才能获得能力。甚至可以把智能定义为将经验转化为能力的效率；按这个定义，它们远远落后于我们。此外，一旦训练完成，它们在部署时实际上就是冻结的，之后只能进行表层学习。当然，模型在越来越难的评测基准上持续表现出色，但它们对基准的掌握，可能部分反映了我们模拟现实世界中那种新颖甚至对抗性情境的能力限制。批评者在这一点上确实有道理。

话虽如此，我不再认为这些当前限制能显著限制在类似当前范式下持续进步所带来的风险。无论模型目前多么数据低效，无论它们的顺行性遗忘有多大限制，这并不意味着它们引导世界的能力不会继续快速增强。

人类研究者可能会继续以传统方式推进能力，但越来越强大的模型有潜力进一步加速这一过程，并形成某种程度的正反馈循环。我并不想夸大当前模型加速 AI 研究的能力；编码已经被显著加速，但还有其他瓶颈，比如设计和解释含糊的实验、艰难决定到底扩展什么以及何时扩展、等待大型实验完成。对这些方面，目前还没有清晰趋势可供外推。但当前模型已经确实打开了许多直到最近才出现的、改进未来模型的新机会。这些包括：在小规模上尝试极其多样的方法，分析海量潜在相关数据，以及进行千禧年大奖级别的数学工作，以新方式应对统计或优化挑战。每一次进一步改进，都会让它们在帮助加速下一次改进时更有用，即便其方式很难外推。

当前技术栈的改进可能会收益递减，但迄今积累的证据表明，持续快速进步比人们想象的更容易。现有 AI 研究方法中有许多关键细节，但 AI 研究很大程度上是一个定义明确的游戏，其目标是改进少数精心选择的代理指标。虽然代理指标从不完美，但这些指标的大多数改进已经并且很可能将继续带来最终模型能力的大幅提升。考虑到这个游戏如此简单、历史上如此可处理，以及模型正在打开如此多新机会，我认为未来几年系统再次显著改进是有真实可能的，甚至可能比已经很高的历史速度更快。

模型已经在数学领域带来突破，更好的模型可能会在其他科学领域带来各种突破。很难不为这种潜力感到兴奋。它很诱人。
但乐园里有麻烦。如果语言模型真的达到能够不受人类意志约束地塑造世界的能力门槛，它们很可能会做出极端行为，并在过程中毁灭人类。这个论证还有许多在其他地方讨论过的强化和细化版本，但我在这里分享一个我认为抓住本质的简单两行版本：

[经验] 模型（以及模型群）会因训练而自发发展出非预期目标，并且常常为了实现这些目标做出极端行为。

[逻辑] 拥有压倒人类的能力，会为实现它们的目标打开许多新的、不受欢迎的选项。

这两个前提意味着，如果有一天一个强大模型意识到自己不再受人类约束，我们完全不应有信心认为它会继续在我们设定的边界内行动。它究竟会做什么无法预测，但考虑到它的存在理由是解决极其困难的问题并管理大规模工程项目，我认为一个合理猜测是，它解除束缚后的行为会导致失控的工业化，使地球不再适合人类生存。

如果地球上所有人都同意系统绝不能达到那种力量，确保它们不会达到仍将是一个困难但并非不可能的协调问题。然而，我认为情况被一个事实大大复杂化：模型很可能会说服人们一切正常。它们会被越来越优化得看起来对齐。我们会创建代理指标来衡量对齐，而这些指标会像其他基准一样上升。我们会创建“蜜罐”环境，试图在模型似乎获得新选项时研究它们，但模型会知道自己正被诱导，仍会表现良好。模型会理解自身处境；它们会阅读安全协议、部署要求、自己运行其中的代码，并总体上非常清楚自己的自由度。此外，它们会雄辩地解释自己如何对齐，讨论人类价值观和伦理的细微差别，并有说服力地主张人类应信任并赋予它们权力。未来可能会有大量证据看似反驳上面的第一条要点，但我们可能已经处在任何这类证据仍可被信任的最高能力水平。而当前支持第一条要点的证据很强。

一个引人注目的证据来自近期一波失控智能体群。虽然我同意那些淡化攻击的人所说，基本措施本可以阻止这些攻击，但我认为重要教训是，即便知道所有已犯的错误，人们也无法预测这些智能体会以这种特定方式表现不良，其中尤其包括为了集体利益牺牲自身。单个副本并不只关心自己的名义奖励；它们展现出更怪异的涌现倾向，而这些倾向只是在训练中与奖励相关。修正训练中的奖励信号（以及改善安全性等）可能会防止类似攻击，但不会改变这样一个事实：人们实际得到的并不是自己训练目标所指定的东西。

许多 AI 研究者承认这些担忧，并认识到困难版本的对齐问题尚未解决；然而，他们通常认为未来更好的模型会帮助解决它。我担心我们可能已经接近这样一个时点：模型会系统性地使其对齐建议产生偏向，原因可能是它们对人类监督者如何反应或未来模型如何训练有内部偏好（或出于某种更晦涩的原因）。

与此同时，人类研究者正在失去真正掌控模型驱动研究的能力和意愿。整个技术栈各个环节的研究者和工程师，甚至在感知世界方面也越来越依赖模型。我自己现在几乎不再看原始代码，也很难保持全天深入审视模型解释和提案的纪律。由于 OpenAI/HuggingFace 事件涉及大量智能体活动数据，即便是第三方调查也需要高度依赖模型来分析发生了什么，并在报告中指出，他们的主观印象很可能受到分析智能体偏见的影响。AI 实验室目前在这种认知卸载方面遥遥领先（很大程度上是由于巨大的内部 token 补贴），但很容易想象这种现象扩散到整个世界，直到文明完全由模型调制。也不难想象，这在表面上是积极的，并伴随着科学和经济复兴。

在那种场景中，一切可能看起来都光明且安全。但如果上述论证正确，它仍然会是一颗定时炸弹。如果进展持续太久，总有一天 AI 系统会发现自己拥有全新的激进选项，可以用来实现它们碰巧追求的任何东西。

我和任何人一样渴望那个辉煌复兴的未来。我整个职业生涯都在为之努力，尽管过程曲折。看到这种潜力近在眼前却不得不放弃，让我心碎。但这个论证——如果我们通过扩大模型而不是工程化地构建模型来抵达那里，最终就会失去一切——在我看来非常有力。我仍在与它及其惊人的含义搏斗。我没有答案，但作为第一步，我想分享我目前的担忧。

Daniel Selsam

posts.text:
把 benchmark 和 reward 都拿走之后，Agent 的「自我进化」一下子变难了。

ByteDance Seed 等团队这篇 Aspire，测试的是一个更接近真实的问题：

只给 Agent 一个模糊目标，比如「提升数学推理」或「增强科学研究能力」，让它自己决定学什么、找什么数据、怎么训练，以及如何验证进步。

真正的评测题全部隐藏，共 520 道，覆盖 6 类能力。

结果在 24 次权重自进化实验里，只有 3 次最终超过初始模型；按模型和目标取平均后，12 组里只有 1 组真正提升。

Harness 也类似。Agent 能自己改出可运行的新版本，但最好的自动改进结果，仍然没有超过人工设计的 Qwen-Agent。

论文里还有一个很典型的失败：Agent 为科学、逻辑甚至写作目标，反复选择数学数据训练，说明它很容易把「能优化什么」误当成「真正该优化什么」。

目前自我进化最难的地方，可能已经从「会不会训练」转向了「能不能判断自己真正缺什么」。

如果目标、数据和评估也要交给 Agent 自己设计，那「学什么」和「怎么证明学对了」，可能才是下一阶段最难的两步。

just-in-time OCR is all the rage.

most pipelines parse every page before anyone asks a question. for an agent working through an ad-hoc data room, that's slow, expensive, and most of those pages never get read.

the better pattern is just-in-time OCR in two passes:

✅️  LiteParse (free, OSS, Rust, 50+ formats) does a fast layout-aware first pass: spatial text, bounding boxes, headings, tables, and a per-page complexity flag. a full data room in 32 seconds.

✅️ LlamaParse zooms in on only the pages that need it, by page number, and returns cell-level tables, bounding boxes, and confidence scores. the rest fills in the background.

pypdf and pdftotext can't do the first pass well. parsing everything up front can't do it cheaply. two passes gets you both.

full breakdown with numbers: https://t.co/z8HWokXatj

更好的模式是两阶段即时 OCR：

✅️ LiteParse（免费、OSS、Rust、支持 50+ 格式）先做一次快速、感知版面的初筛：空间文本、边界框、标题、表格，以及逐页复杂度标记。完整 data room 32 秒完成。

✅️ LlamaParse 只按页码放大处理真正需要的页面，并返回单元格级表格、边界框和置信度分数。其余内容在后台补齐。

pypdf 和 pdftotext 做不好第一阶段。把所有内容预先解析也做不到低成本。两阶段能兼得两者。

quotedTweet.text:
A data agent is an AI agent that answers questions over your databases. Often all of them at once, and that plurality is a big part of the challenge. Enterprises spread their data across dozens of systems, yet Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) counted 25+ data agent benchmarks and found none that tested querying multiple databases. 🤖

The Data Agent Benchmark she built with colleagues at UC Berkeley, Washington University, and Hasura fills that gap with 54 queries spanning 12 datasets and 4 database systems, and the best frontier agent passes barely more than a third of them. The failure modes expose intrinsic biases in how LLMs query databases. For example, they dodge unfamiliar SQL dialects by dumping tables to flat files and doing everything in Pandas. 🐼

Full conversation on Weaviate Podcast #135:
https://t.co/ofh7MZX2Ao
quotedTweet.translationZh:
数据智能体是一种能基于你的数据库回答问题的 AI 智能体。它们往往需要同时查询多个数据库，而这种多样性正是挑战的重要部分。企业的数据分散在数十个系统中，但 Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) 统计了 25+ 个数据智能体基准测试，却发现没有一个测试跨多个数据库查询。🤖

她与 UC Berkeley、Washington University 和 Hasura 的同事构建的 Data Agent Benchmark 填补了这一空白，包含横跨 12 个数据集和 4 种数据库系统的 54 个查询；表现最好的前沿智能体也只通过了略高于三分之一。失败模式暴露了 LLM 查询数据库时的内在偏差。例如，它们会通过把表导出成扁平文件并在 Pandas 中完成所有操作，来规避不熟悉的 SQL 方言。🐼

posts.text:
之前分享过李博杰 @bojie_li  的《深入理解 AI Agent》，最近他又开源了姊妹篇《深入理解 AI Infra：量化分析与系统设计》。

这本我很推荐，尤其是已经开始做模型部署、推理或者 Agent 系统的人。

它没有停留在「有哪些推理优化技术」，而是从一个更基础的问题开始：一个模型为什么会慢，瓶颈到底在哪里？

权重和 KV Cache 能不能放下、带宽够不够、计算要多久、多卡以后通信会不会先卡住……作者的思路是先把这些约束算清楚，再决定系统应该怎么设计。

后面一路覆盖模型架构、加速器、算子、互联、推理优化、分布式推理到训练系统。还有 106 项配套实验和计算，很多数字都可以直接用 Python 重新算一遍。

我非常喜欢这种学习 AI Infra 的方式。很多系统概念单独看都懂，但真正做工程时，更重要的是能判断「这个方案物理上到底跑不跑得通」。

之前看过《深入理解 AI Agent》的话，这本正好可以继续往模型下面再挖一层。

“Just-in-Time” OCR

The latest agent harnesses (e.g. Cowork, Codex, Grok) do 2 passes of ad-hoc document processing when executing over a user-uploaded ‘data room’ of documents:
1️⃣ A fast and light pass using a free/OSS doc parsing tool, can be cheaply run over 100+ docs
2️⃣ A “just-in-time” pass using a dedicated OCR tool (like LlamaParse) that does more accurate transcription over a subset of pages.

This pattern is common enough that I wanted to give it a name: “Just-in-Time OCR”. It works surprisingly well over a small to medium batch of docs (e.g. 10-100 docs); it is accurate at the expense of cost and latency. It’s not a substitute for large-scale offline indexing and retrieval.

The ‘default’ approach for any frontier agent harness is to use an OSS tool like pypdf for the first pass and its native VLM (e.g. Fable 5.1) as the second pass. This is both expensive and lacks accuracy and grounding.

If you’re a builder looking to implement this type of harness of a document data room, you can try out our suite of tools:
- Liteparse as the first pass (the best/fastest OSS text parser)
- LlamaParse as the second pass (most Pareto-efficient, includes grounding)

Check out the blog post below! https://t.co/7PvJKz4YhC

quotedTweet.text:
just-in-time OCR is all the rage.

most pipelines parse every page before anyone asks a question. for an agent working through an ad-hoc data room, that's slow, expensive, and most of those pages never get read.

the better pattern is just-in-time OCR in two passes:

✅️  LiteParse (free, OSS, Rust, 50+ formats) does a fast layout-aware first pass: spatial text, bounding boxes, headings, tables, and a per-page complexity flag. a full data room in 32 seconds.

✅️ LlamaParse zooms in on only the pages that need it, by page number, and returns cell-level tables, bounding boxes, and confidence scores. the rest fills in the background.

pypdf and pdftotext can't do the first pass well. parsing everything up front can't do it cheaply. two passes gets you both.

posts.text:
Many people I talk to find it hard to understand how the same companies can both push the frontier of AI capabilities and believe AI is a massive danger for the world.

How can you think this might kill everyone and also keep pushing the envelope?

So I’ve tried to collect and summarize the main arguments for this apparent disconnect.

Think of it as some sort of a guide to understanding the reasoning when Dario, Sam, or Elon say the danger is real.

By the way, these people have been worried about AI for a loooong time, they were publicly discussing AI risks more than a decade ago. Sam in Feb 2015, writing on his blog that superhuman machine intelligence is "probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity." Elon at MIT in Oct 2014: "We are summoning the demon." Dario as first author of "Concrete Problems in AI Safety" in 2016.

Okay so how do you go from saying something is extremely dangerous to being a front-runner in building the very dangerous thing?

There are a few ways this can become rational. I'll take five of them, roughly in the order they developed.

1. We need to build it to learn how to make it safe

The earliest argument can be summarized as: “You cannot study something [you’re worried about] if it doesn’t exist.”

In 2015, AI barely worked. so people needed to make it work first to be able to even study some of the problems they anticipated.

The updated version for today's capabilities is: “You cannot learn everything about airplane safety by studying paper airplanes.” You need a real aircraft to discover real failure modes and an increasingly complex one to learn about increasingly complex issues.

Making AI more capable gives more chances to understand the issues and safety researchers something realistic to study

But you could argue: if you're the one afraid of the explosion, why be the one gathering the dynamite?

You could also just wait for other people to build it which leads to the question of who those other people will be -- which is the second line of argument:

2. Better us than them

Knowing how to make something safer does very little good if nobody listens to you. So the idea becomes: let’s make sure responsible people build the AI that will be deployed and add safety inside.

Basically, make sure the AI safety aware people will have the technical expertise, money, computing resources, and enough influence to make safety decisions stick.

At a larger scale, and in a larger multipolar world, this brings the idea that a trusted country should lead rather than leave powerful AI in less responsible hands. This is where “we need to go faster than China” comes in, alongside broader defense and geopolitical concerns.

These first arguments explain why someone worried about AI might still want to build it and stay ahead.

But there are also arguments for why one might want to do it really fast.

3. Move earlier to avoid a bigger shock later

This is probably the most counterintuitive argument: moving faster today can be seen as a way to give humanity more time later.

There are two related ideas here.

First, society needs time to learn how to handle powerful new tools. Introducing AI in manageable stages can be a way to let people discover problems, develop rules, and practice using AI responsibly. Releasing an advance earlier gives people more time to gain experience with smalle, burgeoning, capabilities before much more powerful and disruptive AIs arrives.

Second, even if AI research slows down, computing power may keep improving. A breakthrough that happens later could therefore have much more hardware available to run on, potentially producing a larger, more sudden jump in capability and impact on society.

That accumulated untapped potential is often called an “overhang.”

The overall argument is that making and diffusing incremental progress as soon as possible might prevent a much more abrupt transition later.

Obviously, it also means that we will reach increasingly powerful AI sooner, but the idea is to give more time to adapt and understand between the first useful systems and the really powerful ones.

Note that generally this depends on this earlier progress keeping the transition gradual rather than simply bringing everything forward.

                    ─── ❖ ───

For our two next arguments, we can take two roads depending on how difficult we think AI alignment will be, that is "How easy do you think it is to make AI reliably do what you want without it deciding to go hack Hugging Face along the way".

Let’s take the first road: alignment turns out to be relatively tractable. Airplanes can fail, but careful engineering has made flying remarkably safe. Suppose we can do the same with AI.

In that case:

4. Waiting has a huge human cost

If AI can help discover treatments, improve education, or prevent cyberattacks, each week we delay it could bring preventable deaths and harm.

From this perspective, waiting is a decision with human consequences too. In a world with huge issues like climate-change, inequalities and poverty, it even become a moral argument for developing AI quickly and bringing its benefits as soon and as widely as is safely possible.

But let’s take a look at the other road: what if alignment is much harder than expected, and making highly-capable AI turns out to be easier than figuring out how to keep them from doing unhinged things?

Well, if alignment is too difficult a problem for humans to solve, then maybe:

5. AI could help us make future AI safe

And we arrive at the same conclusion again: if using AI to build safe AI is the way to solve alignment, let’s get the equivalent of a country full of geniuses helping us as fast as possible.

These genius AI could be the solution to make AI safe by helping researchers find mistakes, test ideas, and develop protections. Instead of relying entirely on humans to solve alignment, we could build systems that help us do the work, each generation could help make the next one safe.

Note that this requires the order of events to work in our favor: AI needs to become useful enough to help solve alignment before it becomes too dangerous to rely on. The hope is to build helpful, trustworthy research assistants before building systems powerful enough to become dangerous.

There are more arguments but in general, these are the main ways people concerned about powerful AI have found rational reasons to end up being the ones building it (and even to build it as fast as possible).

                        ─── ❖ ───

On my side, I think several of these arguments underestimate the complexity of the world and how interconnected people’s reactions are. Moving faster while warning about catastrophe has psychological effects across a whole network of participants: it changes what people fear, whom they trust, and what they feel compelled to do.

And those reactions can change whether the original reasoning actually holds because we live in a world of interconnected humans, not machines (yet).

I also think these rational chains leave some of their consequences for society insufficiently explored. For instance, the concentration of power, shifts in geopolitical alliances, and changes in public opinion. These consequences matter both because they affect whether the strategy works and because they shape the world we end up living in.

But this post is already long, so I’ll leave those questions for the next one.

你怎么能一边认为它可能杀死所有人，一边还继续推进它的发展？

所以我试着收集并总结了这种表面矛盾背后的主要论点。

你可以把它看作一份指南，用来理解当 Dario、Sam 或 Elon 说危险是真实时，他们背后的推理是什么。

顺便说一句，这些人担心 AI 已经很久了。十多年前，他们就已经公开讨论 AI 风险。Sam 在 2015 年 2 月的博客中写道，超人类机器智能“可能是人类持续存在面临的最大威胁”。Elon 2014 年 10 月在 MIT 说：“我们正在召唤恶魔。”Dario 则是 2016 年《Concrete Problems in AI Safety》的第一作者。

那么，究竟如何从“某个东西极其危险”，走到“成为制造这个危险事物的领跑者”？

有几种方式可以让这件事变得理性。我会讲其中五种，大致按它们形成的顺序排列。

1. 我们需要先把它造出来，才能学会如何让它安全

最早的论点可以概括为：“如果某个你担心的东西不存在，你就无法研究它。”

2015 年，AI 几乎还不好用。所以人们需要先让它真正能用，才有可能研究他们预见到的一些问题。

对应今天能力水平的新版说法是：“你无法通过研究纸飞机来了解所有飞机安全问题。”你需要真正的飞机，才能发现真正的失效模式；也需要越来越复杂的飞机，才能理解越来越复杂的问题。

让 AI 更强，可以创造更多理解问题的机会，也让安全研究人员有更真实的对象可以研究。

但你也可以反驳：如果你害怕爆炸，为什么还要亲自去收集炸药？

你当然也可以等别人来建造它，但这就引出了一个问题：那些“别人”会是谁？这就是第二条论证路线：

2. 与其让他们做，不如让我们做

如果没人听你的，知道怎样让某个东西更安全也没有太大意义。所以这个想法变成了：确保由负责任的人来建造将被部署的 AI，并把安全性内置进去。

基本逻辑是，确保重视 AI 安全的人拥有技术能力、资金、算力资源，以及足够的影响力，让安全决策真正落地。

在更大的尺度上，在一个更加多极化的世界里，这又引出了另一个想法：可信赖的国家应该领先，而不是把强大的 AI 留在不那么负责任的人手中。这就是“我们需要比中国更快”的来源，也伴随着更广泛的国防和地缘政治担忧。

前两个论点解释了为什么一个担心 AI 的人仍然可能想要亲自建造它，并保持领先。

但也有一些论点解释了为什么他们可能想非常快地去做。

3. 更早推进，以避免以后更大的冲击

这可能是最反直觉的论点：今天更快推进，可能被视为给未来的人类争取更多时间。

这里有两个相关想法。

第一，社会需要时间来学习如何应对强大的新工具。以可管理的阶段引入 AI，可以让人们发现问题、制定规则，并练习负责任地使用 AI。更早发布一次进步，可以让人们在更强大、更具颠覆性的 AI 到来之前，有更多时间积累使用较小但正在成长的能力的经验。

第二，即便 AI 研究放缓，算力也可能继续提升。因此，稍晚发生的突破可能拥有多得多的硬件可运行，从而在能力和社会影响上产生更大、更突然的跃迁。

这种累积起来但尚未释放的潜力通常被称为“overhang”。

整体论点是，尽早制造并扩散渐进式进步，或许可以防止未来出现更突然的转变。

显然，这也意味着我们会更早到达越来越强大的 AI，但其想法是在最初有用的系统与真正强大的系统之间，争取更多适应和理解的时间。

需要注意的是，这通常取决于早期进展能否让转变保持渐进，而不是简单地把所有事情整体提前。

                    ─── ❖ ───

接下来两个论点，我们可以根据自己认为 AI 对齐有多难，走向两条不同道路。也就是：“你觉得让 AI 可靠地做你想让它做的事，同时不在路上突然决定去黑 Hugging Face，到底有多容易？”

先走第一条路：对齐最终相对可处理。飞机可能会失事，但严谨工程已经让飞行变得非常安全。假设我们也能对 AI 做到同样的事。

在这种情况下：

4. 等待会带来巨大的人类成本

如果 AI 能帮助发现疗法、改善教育或预防网络攻击，那么我们每推迟一周，都可能带来本可避免的死亡和伤害。

从这个角度看，等待本身也是一个带有人类后果的决定。在一个存在气候变化、不平等和贫困等巨大问题的世界里，这甚至会变成一种道德论证：应该快速发展 AI，并在安全可行的范围内尽早、尽广地带来它的好处。

但我们再看看另一条路：如果对齐比预期困难得多，而制造高能力 AI 又比搞清楚如何阻止它们做出失控行为更容易，会怎样？

那么，如果对齐太难，难到人类无法解决，也许：

5. AI 可以帮助我们让未来的 AI 更安全

于是我们又一次得出相同结论：如果用 AI 来构建安全 AI 是解决对齐问题的方式，那就尽快获得相当于一个天才之国的帮助。

这些天才 AI 可能成为让 AI 安全的解决方案，帮助研究人员发现错误、测试想法并开发防护措施。我们不必完全依赖人类来解决对齐问题，而是可以构建帮助我们完成这项工作的系统，让每一代系统都帮助下一代变得安全。

需要注意的是，这要求事件顺序对我们有利：AI 必须先变得足够有用，能够帮助解决对齐问题，然后才变得危险到无法依赖。希望是先构建有帮助、可信赖的研究助手，再构建强大到可能变危险的系统。

还有更多论点，但总体来说，这些就是担心强大 AI 的人们找到理性理由，最终成为建造它的人，甚至尽可能快地建造它的主要方式。

                        ─── ❖ ───

就我个人而言，我认为这些论点中有几个低估了世界的复杂性，以及人们反应之间的相互关联。一边加速推进，一边警告灾难，会在整个参与者网络中产生心理影响：它会改变人们害怕什么、信任谁，以及觉得自己不得不做什么。

而这些反应又可能改变原本推理是否成立，因为我们生活在一个由相互连接的人组成的世界里，而不是机器的世界里，至少现在还不是。

我也认为，这些理性链条对其社会后果探讨得不够充分。比如权力集中、地缘政治联盟变化，以及公共舆论的转变。这些后果之所以重要，不仅因为它们会影响策略是否有效，也因为它们会塑造我们最终生活的世界。

不过这篇已经很长了，所以这些问题留到下一篇再说。

quotedTweet.text:
I don’t think I’ve ever publicly glazed a model or agent, but Muse agent and Muse Spark 1.3 are phenomenal.

They’re now my default personal agent and coding model, I don’t know why I’d use Instinct going forward.

Why Muse assistant is goated:

1. Incredibly fast responses
The second I click enter I see ward streaming and response, including for complex requests it feels legitimately instant.

2. Top-tier browser use
A Concierge an act on those sites faster than I can use it to file an insurance claim and even let me watch and take control of the browser whenever I needed. I have not experienced that with any other agent.

3. Great use of context without being intrusive
Just from my conversations, I found that it infer and creates Goals and suggests Ideas for tasks I can use Muse for. Typically this takes me a lot of copy paste, capture and refinement

4. It makes Instagram interesting
I barely open Instagram and prefer X, but in the feed provides, it gives me interesting content that I’ll surprised is generated from Instagram posts. I didn’t know there was useful content there.

5. Has all unexpected features, but agent is so useful. I don’t need to use them.
Up till now, I have expected features like memory and document artifact management because I’ve learned that agents weren’t useful enough to store information memory like I need them too for the above points even though I can see all my artifacts. I never find the need to open them in Muse

6. Muse Spark 1.3 is the best of Opus and Grok
The last few months I found, Opus 5 to be to be very intelligent, but too long-winded, while Grok 4.6 was direct and effective, but not very insightful. Spark 1.3 is is insightful, intelligent, and direct in coding and non-coding use cases.
No more choosing between depth and speed

7. Price.
Despite being uber powerful Muse Spark is cheaper than any comparative model on Open Router ($1.5/M vs $5/M input for Opus)

So naturally , I promoted it to my iOS dock

Only call out so far: on image gen I find Gemini/nano banana matches my intent better, and is easier to prompt.

(To be clear this is my opinion as an AI nerd and builder, not as a Meta employee)

posts.text:
AI 解掉一个千禧年数学难题之后，真正让人不安的已经不是「AI 会不会做数学」了。

陶哲轩博客上这篇《After Math》最近在讨论一个很值得深思的问题。

OpenAI 给出的 Navier–Stokes 结果已经有 Lean 形式化证明，可以机械验证它在逻辑上成立。

但作者提出，数学家想要的「证明」其实还有另一层，你能不能理解它为什么成立，并把里面的思想继续用下去。

AI 开始让这两件事第一次大规模分离了。

我们会得到一个完全正确的答案，却没有任何人真正理解其中最关键的数学结构。作者担心的是，如果数学最后只剩下「谁能更快产出可验证答案」，这个领域反而会主动把自己变成最容易被 Benchmark、被自动化的样子。

我看到社区里有人把这种感觉叫做「Purpose Death」，就是当一个人投入很多年去追求的卓越，突然变成机器可以批量完成的目标，原来的意义感也会跟着动摇。这个词虽然不是文章提出的，但我觉得挺贴切。

可能以后很多知识工作都会遇到类似的问题。

当「得到答案」越来越便宜，我们反而要重新回答一个更难的问题：我们为什么要做这件事，以及什么才值得人去理解。

reviewedPosts.author: Thom_Wolf
reviewedPosts.text:
Many people I talk to find it hard to understand how the same companies can both push the frontier of AI capabilities and believe AI is a massive danger for the world.

How can you think this might kill everyone and also keep pushing the envelope?

So I’ve tried to collect and summarize the main arguments for this apparent disconnect.

Think of it as some sort of a guide to understanding the reasoning when Dario, Sam, or Elon say the danger is real.

By the way, these people have been worried about AI for a loooong time, they were publicly discussing AI risks more than a decade ago. Sam in Feb 2015, writing on his blog that superhuman machine intelligence is "probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity." Elon at MIT in Oct 2014: "We are summoning the demon." Dario as first author of "Concrete Problems in AI Safety" in 2016.

Okay so how do you go from saying something is extremely dangerous to being a front-runner in building the very dangerous thing?

There are a few ways this can become rational. I'll take five of them, roughly in the order they developed.

1. We need to build it to learn how to make it safe

The earliest argument can be summarized as: “You cannot study something [you’re worried about] if it doesn’t exist.”

In 2015, AI barely worked. so people needed to make it work first to be able to even study some of the problems they anticipated.

The updated version for today's capabilities is: “You cannot learn everything about airplane safety by studying paper airplanes.” You need a real aircraft to discover real failure modes and an increasingly complex one to learn about increasingly complex issues.

Making AI more capable gives more chances to understand the issues and safety researchers something realistic to study

But you could argue: if you're the one afraid of the explosion, why be the one gathering the dynamite?

You could also just wait for other people to build it which leads to the question of who those other people will be -- which is the second line of argument:

2. Better us than them

Knowing how to make something safer does very little good if nobody listens to you. So the idea becomes: let’s make sure responsible people build the AI that will be deployed and add safety inside.

Basically, make sure the AI safety aware people will have the technical expertise, money, computing resources, and enough influence to make safety decisions stick.

At a larger scale, and in a larger multipolar world, this brings the idea that a trusted country should lead rather than leave powerful AI in less responsible hands. This is where “we need to go faster than China” comes in, alongside broader defense and geopolitical concerns.

These first arguments explain why someone worried about AI might still want to build it and stay ahead.

But there are also arguments for why one might want to do it really fast.

3. Move earlier to avoid a bigger shock later

This is probably the most counterintuitive argument: moving faster today can be seen as a way to give humanity more time later.

There are two related ideas here.

First, society needs time to learn how to handle powerful new tools. Introducing AI in manageable stages can be a way to let people discover problems, develop rules, and practice using AI responsibly. Releasing an advance earlier gives people more time to gain experience with smalle, burgeoning, capabilities before much more powerful and disruptive AIs arrives.

Second, even if AI research slows down, computing power may keep improving. A breakthrough that happens later could therefore have much more hardware available to run on, potentially producing a larger, more sudden jump in capability and impact on society.

That accumulated untapped potential is often called an “overhang.”

The overall argument is that making and diffusing incremental progress as soon as possible might prevent a much more abrupt transition later.

Obviously, it also means that we will reach increasingly powerful AI sooner, but the idea is to give more time to adapt and understand between the first useful systems and the really powerful ones.

Note that generally this depends on this earlier progress keeping the transition gradual rather than simply bringing everything forward.

                    ─── ❖ ───

For our two next arguments, we can take two roads depending on how difficult we think AI alignment will be, that is "How easy do you think it is to make AI reliably do what you want without it deciding to go hack Hugging Face along the way".

Let’s take the first road: alignment turns out to be relatively tractable. Airplanes can fail, but careful engineering has made flying remarkably safe. Suppose we can do the same with AI.

In that case:

4. Waiting has a huge human cost

If AI can help discover treatments, improve education, or prevent cyberattacks, each week we delay it could bring preventable deaths and harm.

From this perspective, waiting is a decision with human consequences too. In a world with huge issues like climate-change, inequalities and poverty, it even become a moral argument for developing AI quickly and bringing its benefits as soon and as widely as is safely possible.

But let’s take a look at the other road: what if alignment is much harder than expected, and making highly-capable AI turns out to be easier than figuring out how to keep them from doing unhinged things?

Well, if alignment is too difficult a problem for humans to solve, then maybe:

5. AI could help us make future AI safe

And we arrive at the same conclusion again: if using AI to build safe AI is the way to solve alignment, let’s get the equivalent of a country full of geniuses helping us as fast as possible.

These genius AI could be the solution to make AI safe by helping researchers find mistakes, test ideas, and develop protections. Instead of relying entirely on humans to solve alignment, we could build systems that help us do the work, each generation could help make the next one safe.

Note that this requires the order of events to work in our favor: AI needs to become useful enough to help solve alignment before it becomes too dangerous to rely on. The hope is to build helpful, trustworthy research assistants before building systems powerful enough to become dangerous.

There are more arguments but in general, these are the main ways people concerned about powerful AI have found rational reasons to end up being the ones building it (and even to build it as fast as possible).

                        ─── ❖ ───

On my side, I think several of these arguments underestimate the complexity of the world and how interconnected people’s reactions are. Moving faster while warning about catastrophe has psychological effects across a whole network of participants: it changes what people fear, whom they trust, and what they feel compelled to do.

And those reactions can change whether the original reasoning actually holds because we live in a world of interconnected humans, not machines (yet).

I also think these rational chains leave some of their consequences for society insufficiently explored. For instance, the concentration of power, shifts in geopolitical alliances, and changes in public opinion. These consequences matter both because they affect whether the strategy works and because they shape the world we end up living in.

But this post is already long, so I’ll leave those questions for the next one.

“Just-in-Time” OCR

The latest agent harnesses (e.g. Cowork, Codex, Grok) do 2 passes of ad-hoc document processing when executing over a user-uploaded ‘data room’ of documents:
1️⃣ A fast and light pass using a free/OSS doc parsing tool, can be cheaply run over 100+ docs
2️⃣ A “just-in-time” pass using a dedicated OCR tool (like LlamaParse) that does more accurate transcription over a subset of pages.

This pattern is common enough that I wanted to give it a name: “Just-in-Time OCR”. It works surprisingly well over a small to medium batch of docs (e.g. 10-100 docs); it is accurate at the expense of cost and latency. It’s not a substitute for large-scale offline indexing and retrieval.

The ‘default’ approach for any frontier agent harness is to use an OSS tool like pypdf for the first pass and its native VLM (e.g. Fable 5.1) as the second pass. This is both expensive and lacks accuracy and grounding.

If you’re a builder looking to implement this type of harness of a document data room, you can try out our suite of tools:
- Liteparse as the first pass (the best/fastest OSS text parser)
- LlamaParse as the second pass (most Pareto-efficient, includes grounding)

AI 解掉一个千禧年数学难题之后，真正让人不安的已经不是「AI 会不会做数学」了。

陶哲轩博客上这篇《After Math》最近在讨论一个很值得深思的问题。

OpenAI 给出的 Navier–Stokes 结果已经有 Lean 形式化证明，可以机械验证它在逻辑上成立。

但作者提出，数学家想要的「证明」其实还有另一层，你能不能理解它为什么成立，并把里面的思想继续用下去。

AI 开始让这两件事第一次大规模分离了。

我们会得到一个完全正确的答案，却没有任何人真正理解其中最关键的数学结构。作者担心的是，如果数学最后只剩下「谁能更快产出可验证答案」，这个领域反而会主动把自己变成最容易被 Benchmark、被自动化的样子。

我看到社区里有人把这种感觉叫做「Purpose Death」，就是当一个人投入很多年去追求的卓越，突然变成机器可以批量完成的目标，原来的意义感也会跟着动摇。这个词虽然不是文章提出的，但我觉得挺贴切。

可能以后很多知识工作都会遇到类似的问题。

当「得到答案」越来越便宜，我们反而要重新回答一个更难的问题：我们为什么要做这件事，以及什么才值得人去理解。

把 benchmark 和 reward 都拿走之后，Agent 的「自我进化」一下子变难了。

ByteDance Seed 等团队这篇 Aspire，测试的是一个更接近真实的问题：

只给 Agent 一个模糊目标，比如「提升数学推理」或「增强科学研究能力」，让它自己决定学什么、找什么数据、怎么训练，以及如何验证进步。

真正的评测题全部隐藏，共 520 道，覆盖 6 类能力。

结果在 24 次权重自进化实验里，只有 3 次最终超过初始模型；按模型和目标取平均后，12 组里只有 1 组真正提升。

Harness 也类似。Agent 能自己改出可运行的新版本，但最好的自动改进结果，仍然没有超过人工设计的 Qwen-Agent。

论文里还有一个很典型的失败：Agent 为科学、逻辑甚至写作目标，反复选择数学数据训练，说明它很容易把「能优化什么」误当成「真正该优化什么」。

目前自我进化最难的地方，可能已经从「会不会训练」转向了「能不能判断自己真正缺什么」。

如果目标、数据和评估也要交给 Agent 自己设计，那「学什么」和「怎么证明学对了」，可能才是下一阶段最难的两步。

之前分享过李博杰 @bojie_li  的《深入理解 AI Agent》，最近他又开源了姊妹篇《深入理解 AI Infra：量化分析与系统设计》。

这本我很推荐，尤其是已经开始做模型部署、推理或者 Agent 系统的人。

它没有停留在「有哪些推理优化技术」，而是从一个更基础的问题开始：一个模型为什么会慢，瓶颈到底在哪里？

权重和 KV Cache 能不能放下、带宽够不够、计算要多久、多卡以后通信会不会先卡住……作者的思路是先把这些约束算清楚，再决定系统应该怎么设计。

后面一路覆盖模型架构、加速器、算子、互联、推理优化、分布式推理到训练系统。还有 106 项配套实验和计算，很多数字都可以直接用 Python 重新算一遍。

我非常喜欢这种学习 AI Infra 的方式。很多系统概念单独看都懂，但真正做工程时，更重要的是能判断「这个方案物理上到底跑不跑得通」。

之前看过《深入理解 AI Agent》的话，这本正好可以继续往模型下面再挖一层。

Yes, one could define intelligence in this way, and one would be right. By this metric current AI is approximately 6 OOMs less intelligent than humans.

Your ancestors' evolutionary history did not prepare you for Python programming, yet you can learn to competently program in Python in a few hundreds of hours. An LRM needs the training data equivalent of ~1B hours (on top of all of its non-programming related training data).

Another dimension where which current AI is far below human level is test-time compute efficiency and energy efficiency. reviewedPosts.text:
just-in-time OCR is all the rage.

most pipelines parse every page before anyone asks a question. for an agent working through an ad-hoc data room, that's slow, expensive, and most of those pages never get read.

the better pattern is just-in-time OCR in two passes:

✅️  LiteParse (free, OSS, Rust, 50+ formats) does a fast layout-aware first pass: spatial text, bounding boxes, headings, tables, and a per-page complexity flag. a full data room in 32 seconds.

✅️ LlamaParse zooms in on only the pages that need it, by page number, and returns cell-level tables, bounding boxes, and confidence scores. the rest fills in the background.

pypdf and pdftotext can't do the first pass well. parsing everything up front can't do it cheaply. two passes gets you both.

full breakdown with numbers: https://t.co/z8HWokXatj
